The block shows its placeholder and then its content either way, so it looks deferred even when the code is still in the initial bundle. Check the build output, not the screen.
A team wraps the dashboard's sales chart, the heaviest component on the page, in

reports the same Initial Total as before, and no new lazy chunk appears in the output. The cause is one line in the dashboard class, added weeks earlier so a toolbar button could export the chart as an image:
The belief: putting a component inside
moves its code out of the main bundle. The block is the instruction, and the bundle shrinks.

It's what the first paragraph of the guide promises: deferrable views reduce the initial bundle size, and the code for the components, directives and pipes inside the block is split into a separate JavaScript file. The behavior on screen confirms it, since the placeholder renders first and the real content arrives later, exactly like a lazy-loaded block should. The template looks right and the page looks right. What neither of them shows is where the code ended up.
The compiler splits per dependency, and only when it's allowed to
For each component, directive and pipe used in the main
block, Angular's compiler emits a dynamic
instead of a static one. That's the whole mechanism behind

here, and it only works if nothing else in the file needs the class right away. So the guide sets two conditions. First, a dependency must be standalone; one declared in an NgModule is loaded eagerly even inside

. That applies to the components you use in the block directly: what they use in turn may still come from NgModules and travels with them into the lazy chunk. Second, a dependency can't be referenced outside the
blocks of the same file; a reference elsewhere in the template, in the class, or in a
query makes it eager. Listing it in the component's
array is fine; that's how the compiler finds it.
When a condition fails, the block still works. Angular simply renders the placeholder, runs the trigger, and then shows content whose code was there all along.
